indiaMissions.title: Schwartz, Tanjore and Vedanayagam Sastriar
indiaMissions.region: Tamil Nadu: Thanjavur (Tanjore), Tiruchirappalli (Trichinopoly), Tirunelveli, Ramanathapuram and the Coromandel coast
indiaMissions.summary: Christian Friedrich Schwartz, a Halle-trained Lutheran pietist, spent 48 years in South India (1750–1798), building congregations at Tiruchirappalli and Thanjavur, becoming a trusted go-between for Indian rulers and the British, and acting as guardian to the future Raja Serfoji II. Around him grew a Tamil Protestant community with its own poets, catechists and pastors — above all the court poet Vedanayagam Sastriar — which also carried caste distinctions into church life and later clashed with missionaries who demanded their abolition.
indiaMissions.story:
Christian Friedrich Schwartz (1726–1798) was born at Sonnenburg in the Neumark of Brandenburg, studied at Halle under the influence of the Francke foundations, and learnt Tamil there before sailing for the Danish enclave of Tranquebar, which he reached in 1750. The Danish-Halle mission was by then more than forty years old and had a Tamil Bible, a press and a small Lutheran church of mixed castes. Schwartz quickly became a fluent Tamil preacher and a skilled debater with Hindu and Muslim interlocutors, and from 1762 he based himself at Tiruchirappalli (Trichinopoly), where he also served the British garrison as chaplain. From 1767 he was formally employed by the Anglican Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK), which funded the 'English mission' while relying on German Lutheran clergy — an early example of Anglican–Lutheran cooperation.

From 1772 Schwartz worked increasingly in Thanjavur, capital of the Maratha kingdom of Tanjore, and settled there in 1778. Within the fort he built Christ Church (completed c. 1779–80), and he founded schools at Thanjavur, Ramanathapuram and Sivaganga that taught in English and Tamil and were supported by grants from the East India Company and local rulers. His reputation for honesty made him a diplomatic intermediary: in 1779 the Madras government sent him as an envoy to Hyder Ali at Srirangapatna, and during the wars of the 1780s villagers and officials alike trusted him to organise food supplies. Raja Tulaja (Thuljaji), dying in 1787, committed his adopted ten-year-old heir Serfoji to Schwartz's guardianship. Schwartz secured Serfoji's succession, which was confirmed by the British in 1798, shortly before his own death at Thanjavur on 13 February 1798. Serfoji, who never became a Christian, commissioned a marble memorial by John Flaxman for Christ Church and wrote an English verse epitaph for his tutor.

Schwartz's networks spread the Tamil Lutheran church southwards. In 1778 he baptised at Palayamkottai a Maratha Brahmin widow known as Clorinda, who in 1785 built the first church there, the nucleus of the later Tirunelveli church. Schwartz trained Tamil catechists and promoted Sattianadan (Satyanathan), a Vellalar convert, who was ordained at Tranquebar in 1790 and led the first large accessions in Tirunelveli. Colleagues such as Johann Philipp Fabricius in Madras (Tamil Bible revision and hymnal), Christian Wilhelm Gericke at Cuddalore and Vepery, and Schwartz's adopted son Johann Caspar Kohlhoff at Thanjavur extended this work. The resulting congregations were small — a few thousand people across the region — but they were the first Protestant churches in India with a settled Indian leadership of catechists, poets, teachers and pastors.

The most remarkable product of this community was Vedanayagam Sastriar (1774–1864), born at Palayamkottai into a Vellalar family that had passed from Catholicism into the Lutheran church. Brought to Thanjavur as a boy and educated by Schwartz, he became head teacher in the mission school, a friend of Serfoji II and, in effect, an 'evangelical poet' at the Tanjore court, where he received the title Sastriar. Writing in classical Tamil genres — the kuravanji drama, the ula, the kummi and devotional song set to Karnatic ragas — he produced a large body of Christian literature, of which the Bethlehem Kuravanji (c. 1800) is the best known; much of it is still sung in Tamil churches. His work showed that Protestant faith could be expressed in fully Tamil literary and musical forms.

The Tanjore church also became the setting for a long dispute over caste. Under the Halle missionaries, Vellalar and other higher-ranked Christians sat apart from Paraiyar and other low-caste Christians, received communion separately or first, and buried their dead separately, while Christians kept caste names, dress and marriage rules. When the Tamil churches passed to the SPCK and then the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel (SPG) in the 1820s, and the Leipzig Mission took up the Lutheran remnant from the 1840s, evangelical Anglicans led by Bishop Daniel Wilson of Calcutta (whose 1833 directive ordered an end to caste distinctions in worship) treated these practices as incompatible with the gospel. Vedanayagam defended the old Tanjore customs as social rather than religious and lost his position in the mission during these disputes; many higher-caste Christians left, joined the Leipzig Lutherans, who were more tolerant of caste usage, or returned to Catholicism. Historians such as D. Dennis Hudson see the episode as a clash between an older, indigenised Tamil evangelical Christianity and a new, more assertive Anglo-evangelical missionary culture.

indiaMissions.title: The Serampore Trio (Carey, Marshman, Ward)
indiaMissions.region: Bengal: Calcutta (Kolkata), Serampore (Danish Frederiksnagore), Malda and Dinajpur; out-stations across north India, Orissa and Burma
indiaMissions.summary: William Carey reached Calcutta in 1793 as the first missionary of the Baptist Missionary Society; joined in 1799–1800 by Joshua Marshman and William Ward, he founded at Danish Serampore a self-supporting missionary community that translated and printed scripture in dozens of Indian languages, pioneered Bengali prose and journalism, opened schools and Serampore College (1818), and campaigned against sati. Converts were few and the mission split from its home society, but Serampore became the symbolic birthplace of the modern Protestant missionary movement.
indiaMissions.story:
William Carey (1761–1834), a Northamptonshire shoemaker and Particular Baptist pastor, published his Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens in 1792 and helped found the Baptist Missionary Society at Kettering that October. With the former East India Company surgeon John Thomas he sailed on the Danish ship Kron Princessa Maria and landed at Calcutta in November 1793 without Company permission. Poverty, illness and the death of his son Peter left his family in distress, and his wife Dorothy suffered a lasting mental breakdown. From 1794 to 1799 Carey managed an indigo factory at Mudnabati near Malda, learning Bengali and Sanskrit and drafting a Bengali New Testament while preaching in surrounding villages with little visible result.

Because the East India Company refused to admit new missionaries, the next Baptist party — Joshua Marshman (1768–1837), a Bristol schoolmaster, his wife Hannah Marshman (1767–1847) and the printer William Ward (1769–1823) — landed in October 1799 at Serampore, a Danish settlement on the Hooghly 25 km above Calcutta, where Governor Ole Bie offered protection. Carey joined them in January 1800. The families lived as a community under a common purse, pooling earnings from schools, printing and later Carey's salary as teacher (from 1801) and professor (from 1807) of Bengali, Sanskrit and Marathi at the Company's College of Fort William. In December 1800 Carey baptised Krishna Pal, a carpenter, and his own son Felix in the Hooghly — the first Bengali Protestant convert — and in 1801 the Bengali New Testament came off Ward's press. The Serampore Form of Agreement (1805) set out the community's principles: knowledge of Indian thought, preaching in the vernacular, scripture translation, schools, training Indian preachers and the eventual formation of self-governing Indian churches.

Translation and printing were Serampore's greatest work. With Indian pandits, above all Mrityunjay Vidyalankar and Ramram Basu, Carey and his colleagues produced grammars, dictionaries and Bible translations: by Carey's death the press had issued the whole Bible or substantial parts of it in some three dozen or more Indian and Asian languages, from Bengali, Sanskrit, Marathi, Hindi and Odia to Assamese, Punjabi and Chinese — though many were rough first drafts later superseded. A fire on 11 March 1812 destroyed the printing office, manuscripts and paper, but the punches for the type were recovered and work resumed within months, with donations pouring in from Britain. Carey's Fort William circle also printed the first books of modern Bengali prose, including Ramram Basu's Raja Pratapaditya Charitra (1801), and editions of Sanskrit classics such as the Ramayana. In 1818 Serampore launched the Bengali periodical Digdarshan and the newspaper Samachar Darpan, and the English Friend of India.

The trio's schools and social campaigns reached well beyond the small Baptist church. Hannah Marshman ran boarding schools and pioneered education for girls, and Joshua Marshman's Hints Relative to Native Schools (1816) led to a network of vernacular elementary schools in Bengal. Carey organised a count of sati (widow-burning) around Calcutta from 1803 and the Serampore men publicised the practice in Britain; when Lord William Bentinck abolished sati by Regulation XVII of December 1829, Carey translated the regulation into Bengali. Carey also founded the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India (1820) and kept a celebrated botanic garden. In 1818 the trio founded Serampore College to train Indian Christians and others in arts and theology through Indian languages and English; in 1827 King Frederick VI of Denmark granted it a royal charter with power to confer degrees.

Serampore's limitations were also real. Converts were few — mostly from low-ranked and poor Bengali communities, with some Muslims and a handful of Brahmins — and the church remained small and dependent. William Ward's View of the History, Literature and Mythology of the Hindoos (1811; enlarged 1815–20) offered detailed ethnography but described Hindu practice in scathing terms that coloured British attitudes for decades. After the deaths of the founding BMS leaders Andrew Fuller (1815) and John Sutcliff, younger missionaries in Calcutta resented Serampore's independence and control of property; the quarrel led to formal separation of the 'Serampore Mission' from the BMS in 1827 and reunion only in 1837, after Marshman's death. Denmark sold Serampore to Britain in 1845.

The trio's legacy proved larger than their church. Their methods — vernacular translation, printing, schools, the study of Indian languages and religions, Indian evangelists and the goal of an indigenous church — became the template for nineteenth-century Protestant missions. Serampore College's charter, confirmed by the Bengal government's Serampore College Act of 1918, still enables its Senate to award degrees to theological colleges across India and neighbouring countries. Bengali writers have long acknowledged Carey's role in the formation of modern Bengali prose, even while debating how far missionary scholarship served colonial knowledge.

indiaMissions.title: Chaplains, the East India Company and the Charter Act of 1813
indiaMissions.region: Bengal and Bihar (Calcutta, Dinapore), the Ganges valley (Cawnpore), Madras, Bombay; debates in London
indiaMissions.summary: Until 1813 the East India Company kept missionaries out of its territories, fearing that religious interference would provoke revolt. A group of evangelical Company chaplains — David Brown, Claudius Buchanan, Henry Martyn and Thomas Thomason — and their Clapham allies Charles Grant and William Wilberforce campaigned to change this. The Charter Act of 1813 allowed licensed missionaries into British India, created the bishopric of Calcutta and committed public money to education; the Act of 1833 removed the licence requirement.
indiaMissions.story:
The East India Company was a trading corporation that became a territorial power after Plassey (1757). Its directors believed that their rule depended on not offending Hindu and Muslim religious sensibilities, and they actively supported temples, festivals and pilgrimage sites through taxes and patronage. Missionaries without licences could be deported, as several Baptists and American Congregationalists discovered, and the Company's own Anglican chaplains were appointed to serve British soldiers and civilians, not to preach to Indians. Yet a small group of evangelical chaplains, many sponsored by Charles Simeon of Holy Trinity, Cambridge, used these posts to promote Christian teaching, translation and schools.

David Brown (1763–1812), who arrived in 1786, ran the Calcutta orphan school and the Old Church, and became provost of Fort William College. Claudius Buchanan (1766–1815), vice-provost of the college from 1800, sponsored oriental translations, published a Memoir on the Expediency of an Ecclesiastical Establishment for British India (1805), and in 1806–07 toured the south, visiting the St Thomas Christians of Travancore and the Jagannath festival at Puri. His Christian Researches in Asia (1811) painted Hindu practice in lurid terms and became a bestseller that fed public demand for missions. Henry Martyn (1781–1812), a Cornish senior wrangler and Simeon's protégé, served as chaplain at Dinapore (1806) and Cawnpore (1809), translating the New Testament into Hindustani (Urdu), revising Persian and Arabic versions, and gathering a few converts, notably the Muslim scholar Sheikh Salih, baptised as Abdul Masih in 1811. He left India in 1810 to perfect his Persian New Testament at Shiraz and died at Tokat in Anatolia in October 1812, aged 31; his journals made him a model of missionary self-sacrifice for generations.

In London, Charles Grant (1746–1823), a former Company servant converted in Bengal and later chairman of the Company's court of directors, wrote Observations on the State of Society among the Asiatic Subjects of Great Britain (1792), arguing that Britain had a duty to bring Christianity and Western knowledge to India. With William Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect he tried to insert 'pious clauses' into the Company's 1793 charter renewal, but the directors defeated them. The Vellore Mutiny of 1806, in which Indian sepoys killed British officers after dress regulations offended their religious customs, was blamed by some on missionary activity and strengthened the anti-missionary party, whose pamphleteers warned that preaching would cost Britain its empire.

The charter renewal of 1813 became a national campaign. Evangelical Anglicans, Baptists, Methodists and others organised hundreds of petitions to Parliament, and Wilberforce spoke at length in the Commons in June 1813, depicting Hindu society as cruel and degraded. The resulting Charter Act (53 Geo. III c. 155) allowed persons wishing to go to India 'for the purpose of introducing useful knowledge, and of religious and moral improvement' to apply for licences through the Board of Control, established a bishop of Calcutta with three archdeacons, and set aside not less than one lakh of rupees a year for the revival of literature and the promotion of science among Indians. The first bishop, Thomas Fanshaw Middleton, arrived in 1814 and founded Bishop's College, Calcutta (1820); his successor Reginald Heber (bishop 1823–26) toured north and south India and died at Trichinopoly in 1826.

The Act opened the way for the Church Missionary Society, the London Missionary Society, the Wesleyan Methodists, the American Board and others to work openly in British India, although licences could still be refused and Company officials remained cautious. The 1833 Charter Act abolished the licensing system, admitted missionaries of any nationality, and led to the creation of the dioceses of Madras (1835) and Bombay (1837). Evangelicals then turned to ending the Company's 'connection with idolatry' — its management of temple funds and pilgrim taxes at places such as Puri and Gaya — which was gradually dismantled from the late 1830s, the pilgrim tax being abolished in 1840. The debates of 1793–1833 fixed the terms of a lasting argument: whether British rule should be religiously neutral or actively Christian, and whether missions were allies or embarrassments of empire.

indiaMissions.title: Alexander Duff and the English-education strategy in Bengal
indiaMissions.region: Bengal (Calcutta), with parallel Scottish and CMS colleges in Bombay, Madras, Nagpur and Masulipatnam
indiaMissions.summary: Alexander Duff, the Church of Scotland's first missionary to India, arrived in Calcutta in 1830 and opened a school that taught Western subjects and the Bible through English to upper-caste Hindu boys, hoping to undermine Hinduism intellectually and win the elite who would then influence the masses. His converts were few but prominent, his method was copied by Scottish and other missions across India, and he helped shape the colonial decision for English education and the founding of Indian universities.
indiaMissions.story:
Alexander Duff (1806–1878) grew up at Moulin in Perthshire, studied at St Andrews under Thomas Chalmers, and in 1829 was appointed the first missionary of the Church of Scotland. His voyage was disastrous: the Lady Holland was wrecked near Cape Town in February 1830, and he lost his library, before a second near-wreck at the mouth of the Hooghly. Arriving in Calcutta in May 1830, he rejected the existing pattern of vernacular preaching to the poor. He argued instead that Hinduism was bound up with false science and history, which modern Western learning taught in English would dissolve; Christianity, taught alongside it, could fill the vacuum. Converts from the educated classes would then carry the faith 'downward' through Indian society.

On 13 July 1830 Duff opened the General Assembly's Institution on Chitpur Road, in a house provided with the help of the reformer Rammohun Roy, who supported English education though he did not accept orthodox Christianity. Pupils from Brahmin, Kayastha and other upper-caste families flocked to learn English, because English opened doors to government service and commerce. Duff taught a graded curriculum from the alphabet to university-level science, philosophy and political economy, with daily Bible instruction. He also delivered public lectures in 1830–31 aimed at the 'Young Bengal' students of Hindu College, disciples of Henry Derozio who had already abandoned orthodox Hinduism for rationalism.

The first conversions came from this circle. Mohesh Chunder Ghose and Krishna Mohan Banerjee (1813–1885), a Kulin Brahmin and Derozian editor, were baptised in 1832; Banerjee became an Anglican priest, a professor at Bishop's College and a noted Sanskrit scholar. Others followed — Gopinath Nundi, Anundo Chund Mazumdar, and later Lal Behari Day (1824–1892), who became a minister and the author of Bengal Peasant Life (1874). Each baptism provoked crisis: families mourned, pupils were withdrawn, and the Hindu press attacked the mission. Duff's converts were never more than a few dozen, but they formed an influential Bengali Christian intelligentsia.

Duff's influence on policy was considerable. He sided with the 'Anglicists' against the 'Orientalists' in the debate over whether government funds should support Sanskrit and Persian learning or English education; Thomas Babington Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education of February 1835 and Lord William Bentinck's resolution of March 1835 settled the matter in favour of English. Later Duff gave evidence before Parliament during the 1853 charter debates, helped shape Charles Wood's Education Despatch of 1854, which introduced grants-in-aid open to mission schools, and was among the founders of the University of Calcutta in 1857.

The Disruption of 1843 in the Church of Scotland split the mission: Duff and all his fellow missionaries joined the new Free Church, lost their buildings to the Established Church, and opened a new Free Church Institution in 1844. The two Scottish colleges were reunited in 1908 and later became the Scottish Church College, Calcutta. Duff's model spread rapidly: John Wilson founded what became Wilson College in Bombay, John Anderson opened the General Assembly's School in Madras in 1837 (later Madras Christian College), Stephen Hislop founded a school at Nagpur in 1844 (later Hislop College), and the CMS missionary Robert Noble opened a high school at Masulipatnam in 1843 (later Noble College). In Madras and Bombay, as in Calcutta, the baptism of a few high-caste students in 1839–43 caused mass withdrawals of pupils and public protests.

By the later nineteenth century the strategy had produced many colleges but few converts, and critics within the missions — including Rufus Anderson of the American Board and many evangelists — argued that education had become an end in itself. Supporters such as William Miller of Madras Christian College reframed it as 'preparation' that would Christianise Indian thought indirectly. The Christian colleges did educate many leaders of modern India, Hindu, Muslim and Christian alike, and contributed to the Bengal Renaissance and Indian nationalism, while the downward-filtration theory of conversion largely failed: Indian Christianity was to grow mainly through the mass movements of the poor rather than through the elite.

indiaMissions.title: Tirunelveli and Travancore: Ringeltaube, Rhenius, Nadar conversions and the breast-cloth struggle
indiaMissions.region: Southern Tamil Nadu (Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi districts) and South Travancore (now Kanniyakumari district, Tamil Nadu, and southern Kerala)
indiaMissions.summary: In the far south of India, Protestant Christianity grew from Clorinda's small congregation at Palayamkottai into the first large-scale group conversions in Indian Protestant history, chiefly among the Nadars (then called Shanars), palmyra-climbers ranked low in the caste order. Lutheran, CMS, SPG and LMS missionaries — notably Ringeltaube, Rhenius, Mead and Caldwell — built Christian villages, schools and churches, and Nadar Christian women's demand to cover their breasts sparked the Travancore 'breast-cloth' (upper-cloth) struggle of 1813–1859, a landmark in the fight against caste-based dress codes.
indiaMissions.story:
Christianity in the far south had old Catholic roots among the Paravar fishers of the coast, but Protestant work began in the 1770s–80s with Schwartz's visits to Palayamkottai, the baptism of the Maratha Brahmin widow Clorinda and her church of 1785. From 1797 the Tamil pastor Sattianadan, with the catechist David Sundaranandam — himself a Nadar — preached in the palmyra country of the south, where Nadars (then known as Shanars) tapped toddy and made jaggery under the dominance of landholding castes. Whole kin groups began to seek baptism: in 1799 Sundaranandam founded the Christian village of Mudalur ('first village'), and by 1802–03 several thousand people had been baptised under Sattianadan and the Halle missionary Johann Daniel Jaenicke. Persecution by local landholders and the lack of teachers led many to lapse, but a core of Christian villages survived.

Across the mountains in the princely state of Travancore, the London Missionary Society entered the south through William Tobias Ringeltaube (1770–c. 1816), a Prussian pietist who arrived in 1806 at the invitation of Maharasan Vedamanickam, a convert from the village of Mylaudy who had been to Tanjore. Ringeltaube lived in extreme simplicity, built churches at Mylaudy and other villages, and baptised several hundred people, mostly Nadars and others of low status, before leaving in poor health in 1816; he disappeared, probably dying at sea. The British Resident, Colonel John Munro (1810–1819), who was also dewan of Travancore for a time, gave the LMS land and protection at Nagercoil, and Charles Mead (1792–1873) and Richard Knill built a network of congregations, schools and a seminary there from 1818. Munro also supported the CMS 'Mission of Help' to the Syrian Christians at Kottayam from 1816.

In Tirunelveli the CMS took over the Lutheran congregations and sent the Prussian Lutheran Charles Rhenius (1790–1838), who arrived at Palayamkottai in 1820. Rhenius was an energetic organiser and translator; he multiplied village schools and catechists, founded Christian villages such as Dohnavur (1827, named after the Prussian Count Dohna who funded it) and set up societies to buy land and protect converts. Congregations rose from a few thousand to more than ten thousand adherents in his time. In 1835 he broke with the CMS over Anglican ordination and church order and continued independently until his death in 1838; his followers were later reabsorbed. Under the CMS and the SPG, the Tirunelveli church kept growing through group movements, especially after the great famine of 1876–78, when many thousands joined. Missionary scholars there included Robert Caldwell (1814–1891) at Idaiyangudi, whose Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian Languages (1856) transformed linguistics, and G. U. Pope at Sawyerpuram, later translator of the Tirukkural.

The most dramatic social conflict was the breast-cloth (upper-cloth) controversy in South Travancore. Customary law there forbade women of Nadar and other lower-ranked communities to cover their upper bodies in the manner of Nair and other high-caste women, as a mark of subordination. Christian Nadar women, encouraged by missionaries' notions of modesty, began to wear a jacket or an upper cloth across the breast. In 1813 Munro issued an order permitting Christian women to cover themselves, but it was soon qualified, and high-caste opponents attacked women in public, tearing off their cloths. Disturbances broke out in 1822, 1827–29 and most seriously in 1858–59, when Nadar Christians and Hindus together asserted the right and riots spread across South Travancore, with chapels and schools burnt. Under pressure from LMS missionaries and the Madras governor Sir Charles Trevelyan, Maharaja Uthram Thirunal issued a proclamation on 26 July 1859 allowing Nadar women to wear a jacket or to cover their breasts with a coarse cloth, though not in the style of high-caste women; full freedom in dress came only later.

The Nadar conversions and the breast-cloth struggle remain contested in historiography. Missionaries and many Nadar Christians saw them as liberation from caste oppression; Robert Caldwell's ethnography The Tinnevelly Shanars (1849), however, described the community in demeaning terms that Nadar leaders long resented. Historians such as Robert Hardgrave and Dick Kooiman show that conversion was one of several routes by which Nadars pursued upward mobility, alongside the Hindu reform movement of Ayya Vaikundar (Ayyavazhi) and later caste associations; Susan Bayly emphasises continuities between Christian and local religious practice. Christian Nadars became one of the most educated and prosperous communities of the region, while the churches continued to wrestle with caste divisions between Nadar, Vellalar, Paraiyar and other Christians.

indiaMissions.title: American missions: Madura, Arcot (the Scudders), Ahmednagar
indiaMissions.region: Maharashtra (Bombay, Ahmednagar), Tamil Nadu (Madurai, Dindigul, Kodaikanal, Vellore, Arcot), Andhra Pradesh (Chittoor, Madanapalle), Punjab and Uttar Pradesh
indiaMissions.summary: American Protestant missions began in India in 1813 when the first American Board (ABCFM) missionaries landed in Calcutta and moved to Bombay. Over the next century the American Board built the Marathi mission centred on Ahmednagar and the Madura mission in Tamil Nadu, the Scudder family founded the Reformed Church's Arcot mission and pioneered medical work, and American Presbyterians, Methodists, Baptists and Lutherans spread across north and south India — bringing their own democratic, voluntarist style along with schools, colleges, hospitals and a characteristic hostility to caste.
indiaMissions.story:
The first American missionaries to India — Adoniram and Ann Judson, Samuel Newell, Samuel Nott, Gordon Hall and Luther Rice — sailed in 1812 under the newly formed American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM), arriving at Calcutta during the war of 1812 between Britain and the United States. The Company ordered them to leave: the Judsons and Rice became Baptists and went to Burma, while Hall and Nott slipped away to Bombay in 1813, where they were threatened with deportation until the governor, Sir Evan Nepean, allowed them to stay in 1815. The Bombay (later Marathi) mission opened schools and printed Marathi scripture; it expanded to Ahmednagar in 1831, which became its main centre. The Ahmednagar church developed relatively strong Indian leadership, organised congregations under Indian pastors from the 1850s, and later produced figures such as the poet Narayan Vaman Tilak.

In 1816 the ABCFM opened a mission in Jaffna, Ceylon, where its Batticotta Seminary trained Tamil Christians; from there missionaries crossed to Madurai in 1834 to found the Madura mission. Its stations at Madurai, Dindigul, Periyakulam, Tirumangalam and elsewhere spread through the Tamil hinterland. The mission insisted, unlike the Tanjore Lutherans, that converts and church workers renounce caste distinctions, and in 1847 it required its agents to show this by eating food prepared by people of other castes — provoking the withdrawal of many higher-caste Christians. Converts came largely from the Shanar (Nadar), Paraiyar and Pallar communities and some Maravar and Kallar villages. The mission opened the Pasumalai seminary (1842), which grew into the American College, Madurai (1881), and a hill station at Kodaikanal (1845) that later housed the Kodaikanal International School (1901).

The Scudder family became the best-known American missionary dynasty in India. Dr John Scudder Sr (1793–1855), a New York physician, went to Ceylon in 1819 as the ABCFM's first medical missionary and moved to Madras in 1836; his tracts and visits to the United States inspired many young Americans. Seven of his sons became missionaries in India. In 1853–54 his sons, led by Henry Martyn Scudder, organised the Arcot mission in the North Arcot district under the Reformed (Dutch) Church in America, with stations at Arcot, Vellore, Chittoor, Madanapalle and Arni. The Arcot mission combined preaching tours, village schools and medical work; its theological seminary (1887) and high schools trained Tamil and Telugu Christian leaders. Ida Scudder (1870–1960), John Sr's granddaughter, founded the women's medical work at Vellore in 1900 that became the Christian Medical College.

The American Board's leadership also shaped mission theory. In 1854–55 its secretary Rufus Anderson visited India and, with Henry Venn of the CMS, championed the 'three-self' ideal of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches. His deputation pressed the Marathi and Madura missions to cut back English education, close some boarding schools and ordain Indian pastors for village churches — a policy welcomed by some Indian Christians as a step to autonomy but resented by others who valued English schooling as a route to advancement.

Other American churches followed. The Presbyterian Church in the USA founded its Lodiana (Ludhiana) mission in 1834, the first in the Punjab, and later Forman Christian College in Lahore (1864). The Methodist Episcopal Church sent William Butler, who began at Bareilly in 1856, just before the uprising of 1857; the mission later spread across north India under James Thoburn, and Isabella Thoburn opened a girls' school at Lucknow in 1870 that became Isabella Thoburn College (1886), the first Christian women's college in Asia. American Baptists took up the Telugu 'Lone Star' mission at Nellore (1840) and Ongole (1866), and the Lutheran 'Father' J. C. F. Heyer began at Guntur in 1842. By the early twentieth century American missionaries, many recruited through the Student Volunteer Movement, were among the largest foreign contingents in India.

American missions contributed strongly to education, medicine and women's work, and their congregational and democratic instincts encouraged Indian church self-government. They also shared the paternalism of their age: Indian pastors were paid far less than missionaries and long kept out of mission councils, and American mission compounds created dependencies that outlasted independence. Most of these missions were absorbed into the Church of South India (1947) — including the Madura and Arcot churches — and the Church of North India (1970), while Methodist, Baptist and Lutheran churches remained separate.

indiaMissions.title: Dalit mass movements (Punjab Chuhras, Andhra Malas and Madigas, 1870–1930)
indiaMissions.region: Punjab (now partly Pakistan), Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (Ongole, Nellore, Guntur, Godavari, Dornakal, Medak), western Uttar Pradesh (Rohilkhand) and parts of Tamil Nadu
indiaMissions.summary: Between about 1870 and 1930 hundreds of thousands of Dalits — Chuhras in the Punjab, Madigas and Malas in the Telugu country, Chamars in north India and others — joined Christian churches in group or 'mass' movements, usually through kinship networks and Indian lay evangelists rather than missionary preaching. These movements transformed Indian Christianity into a predominantly Dalit church, raised literacy and dignity among the converts, provoked fierce debate among missionaries, Hindu reformers and Gandhi, and were analysed in J. Waskom Pickett's landmark Christian Mass Movements in India (1933).
indiaMissions.story:
Missionaries had long hoped to convert India through its elites, but from the 1870s the decisive growth came from the bottom of the caste order. Group conversion was not new — the Paravars in the sixteenth century and the Nadars of Tirunelveli in the early nineteenth had joined churches as communities — but the scale was. Dalit communities, regarded as 'untouchable' and held in agricultural servitude, often decided collectively, through kin and caste councils, to accept baptism. Their motives combined religious conviction, the search for dignity and education, protection from landlords, and the hope of escaping the stigma of untouchability; missionaries were frequently surprised and divided by the movements.

In the Punjab the movement began with Ditt, a short, lame Chuhra (hereditary sweeper and agricultural labourer) who dealt in hides in the Sialkot district. In 1873 he sought baptism from the United Presbyterian missionary Samuel Martin at Sialkot and, refusing to stay at the mission, went back to his village and brought his relatives to faith. Through Chuhra kinship networks the movement spread across Sialkot, Gujranwala, Gurdaspur and Lahore districts, involving the United Presbyterian, American Presbyterian, CMS, Church of Scotland, Methodist and Salvation Army missions. Within a few decades most Chuhras of the central Punjab districts had become Christians, and the Punjab church — which had numbered only a few thousand Indian Christians in 1881 — grew into a community of several hundred thousand by 1931, overwhelmingly of Chuhra origin. The Punjabi Zabur, a metrical psalter in Punjabi folk tunes (completed 1908), became the heart of their worship.

In the Telugu country the American Baptist 'Lone Star' mission at Nellore had nearly been abandoned before John E. Clough founded the Ongole station in 1866 and found a responsive Madiga community, partly through the Madiga leader Yerraguntla Periah. During the great famine of 1876–78 Clough took a government contract to dig part of the Buckingham Canal, employing thousands of famine-stricken people, and refused baptism until relief was over. When baptisms resumed, 2,222 people were baptised on 3 July 1878 at Velampalli on the Gundlakamma river, and around nine thousand within a few weeks; the Ongole church became for a time one of the largest Baptist churches in the world. Malas and Madigas also joined Lutheran (Guntur, Rajahmundry), CMS (Ellore, Masulipatnam), SPG, LMS (Cuddapah) and Methodist (Hyderabad, Medak) missions. In the Anglican diocese of Dornakal, founded in 1912 under V. S. Azariah, the first Indian Anglican bishop, Mala and Madiga movements produced a church of more than two hundred thousand by the 1930s, while the Wesleyan Charles Posnett's work among Malas and Madigas led to the building of Medak Cathedral (1914–24) partly as famine-relief employment.

In north India the Methodist Episcopal mission, under Bishop James Thoburn, baptised large numbers of Chamars, Mazhabi Sikhs and Balmikis in Rohilkhand and the Punjab from the 1880s, sometimes with minimal instruction, drawing criticism from other missions. Parallel movements among Adivasi peoples — the Oraons and Mundas of Chota Nagpur through the Gossner and Jesuit missions, and peoples of the north-east — added further numbers. Census figures show the scale of change: India's Christian population rose from about 2.9 million in 1901 to about 6.3 million in 1931, with much of the Protestant growth coming through these movements.

The movements generated intense controversy. Many missionaries feared 'unready' converts and inadequate teaching; others defended group conversion as the natural Indian pattern. Arya Samaj reformers in the Punjab answered with shuddhi reconversion campaigns, and the politics of numbers under separate electorates sharpened tension. Mahatma Gandhi in the 1930s opposed missionary efforts among 'Harijans', arguing that they could not understand the change of religion and that conversion divided Hindu society; he clashed on this with missionary leaders and with B. R. Ambedkar, who in 1935 declared he would not die a Hindu and was courted by Christian, Muslim, Sikh and Buddhist leaders before choosing Buddhism in 1956.

In 1928 the National Christian Council commissioned the American Methodist J. Waskom Pickett to survey the movements. His Christian Mass Movements in India (1933) found that converts in group movements generally showed real improvements in literacy, health, cleanliness and freedom from fear, and that group conversion produced more stable churches than isolated individual conversions. The study shaped Azariah's and others' strategy and inspired Donald McGavran's Church Growth theory. Yet the movements also left lasting problems: Dalit Christians often remained landless labourers, faced violence and boycott, and encountered caste discrimination within the churches themselves, while after independence the Presidential Order of 1950 excluded Christian Dalits from Scheduled Caste benefits.

indiaMissions.legacy: The Dalit mass movements are the main reason Indian Christianity today is largely a church of Dalits and Adivasis. They brought education and dignity to communities long excluded, but also set the terms of continuing controversies — over motives for conversion, caste within the church and the denial of Scheduled Caste rights to Dalit Christians — that remain central to Indian public life.
